title: Find £200 With a Ten-Minute Money Audit
meta_description: Run a ten-minute UK spending audit to find unused subscriptions, stale contracts, avoidable fees and safer household-bill savings.

module_headings.external_sources: Primary UK Billing and Consumer Sources

sections.heading: Start With a Ten-Minute Triage, Not a Punishment Budget
paragraphs: The promise of finding £200 a month should be treated as a search target, not a guarantee. Some households have several stale contracts; others have already cut hard. The useful method is to rank recurring costs by potential saving and effort, then verify every result before counting it.

Set a ten-minute timer for discovery only. Open the latest current-account statement, credit-card statement and banking app list of regular payments. Do not cancel while scanning. Capture merchant, amount, frequency and next payment in one list so urgency does not replace judgement.

Begin with repeated amounts, unfamiliar merchant names, annual renewals and bills that changed. A £3 purchase is rarely the first priority. A £55 service no longer used, an out-of-contract broadband bill or duplicated insurance can create more room with one decision.

Sort each line into five actions: keep, cancel after checking, renegotiate or switch, investigate, and protect. “Protect” covers rent or mortgage, Council Tax, energy, essential connectivity, insurance required for work and priority debts. The audit must not create a larger consequence to produce a cosmetic saving.

Use monthly equivalents. Divide an annual bill by twelve, multiply a weekly cost by 52 and divide by twelve, and treat four-weekly payments as thirteen payments a year. A service costing £19 every four weeks is about £20.58 a calendar month, not £19.

Distinguish a price reduction from a cash-flow shift. Paying insurance annually may lower total cost but requires cash now. Moving a bill date may help timing without reducing annual expense. A cashback offer is not a saving until eligibility, fees and payout are confirmed.

Write a baseline before taking action: current monthly equivalent, expected replacement cost, one-off exit or setup fee, and the month the change begins. Without this, a retention discount or free introductory period can look better than it is.

The opening photograph shows receipts and a calculator because the audit starts with evidence. Memory usually remembers large purchases and overlooks small automatic charges, annual renewals and merchant names that differ from the service brand.

If the statement shows missed essential bills, unauthorised transactions or borrowing for food, stop the speed exercise. Use the bill-priority and debt-support route instead. [[S1|MoneyHelper explains]] that some bills carry more serious consequences and should be handled before non-priority spending.
At ten minutes, keep the list even if it totals only £27. A verified £27 recurring saving is more valuable than an invented £200. The next stages turn candidates into safe, documented changes.

sections.heading: Build the Evidence Stack Before Calling Anyone
paragraphs: For each high-value candidate, gather the latest bill, contract end date, notice period, usage and payment method. For insurance add renewal date and cover details. For broadband add speed, data and equipment obligations. For energy add tariff, annual consumption and meter information.

Search twelve months when possible. A one-month statement misses yearly software, roadside assistance, professional memberships, school costs, vehicle tax and insurance. Calendar search and email receipts can reveal renewals that are absent from the current banking screen.

Identify whether a payment is a Direct Debit, standing order, recurring card payment, bank transfer or card purchase. These methods have different cancellation mechanics. Stopping the payment instruction does not automatically end the underlying contract or erase money owed.

[[S2|MoneyHelper’s payment guide]] says a Direct Debit can be cancelled through the bank, while a standing order is an instruction set by the account holder. A recurring card payment uses card details and may continue after a replacement card, depending on the arrangement.

Look up unfamiliar merchants safely. Use the transaction reference, official app, bill or a known website—not a telephone number in an unexpected text. A trading name can differ from the consumer brand, and a card processor can obscure the underlying service.

Mark household ownership. A partner may use a subscription that appears dormant; a family mobile plan may cover several lines; a cloud service may store irreplaceable files. Ask before cancelling shared services and export data before closing storage or software accounts.

Measure use without pretending every low-frequency service is waste. Breakdown cover, insurance and backup storage exist for risk rather than daily entertainment. The question is whether the product is needed, duplicated, correctly sized and competitively priced.

Create a comparison unit. Broadband offers need total contract cost, speed and setup fees. Insurance needs equivalent cover and excess. Groceries need price per kilogram or litre. A lower monthly headline can hide a longer term, weaker cover or smaller package.

Record the source and date of every quote because prices expire. Screenshots are useful, but keep personal and financial data secure. Never publish account numbers, policy documents or full statements in a price-comparison forum.
The evidence stack is complete when another adult could understand the current deal, alternative, change cost and deadline. That discipline makes a ten-minute scan actionable instead of impulsive.

sections.heading: Stop Zombie Renewals Without Breaking Contracts
paragraphs: Subscriptions are the quickest category to inspect because the service, amount and renewal are often visible in an account page. Search streaming, apps, storage, news, gaming, fitness, meal plans, memberships and free trials converted to paid plans.

Classify each as used weekly, used occasionally for a defined reason, duplicated, forgotten or essential. Cancel forgotten and duplicated services first. Rotate entertainment services only if everyone affected agrees and saved profiles or purchases will remain accessible.

Check the minimum term and notice requirement before pressing cancel. A gym, software or education subscription can remain payable after access stops. Record the final service date, final charge and cancellation confirmation.

[[S3|The FCA explains]] that a recurring card payment, also called a continuous payment authority, can be cancelled through the business or card issuer. The issuer must stop it when properly instructed, but cancelling the payment does not necessarily cancel the contract.

Direct Debit cancellation is not a dispute strategy. Contact the supplier when a valid contract remains, especially for credit, utilities, insurance or telecoms. An unpaid bill can trigger arrears, fees, collection activity, service loss or credit-file harm.

Before accepting a retention offer, compare its total cost and new commitment. A half-price month followed by eleven full-price months may be inferior to leaving. Ask whether accepting restarts a minimum term and save the transcript.

Remove stored card details and marketing renewal prompts only after contractual cancellation is confirmed. Deleting an app does not cancel its subscription. For app-store billing, check the platform subscription menu rather than the service app alone.

Annual renewals deserve a diary alert four to six weeks ahead, adjusted to the actual notice period. MoneyHelper recommends reviewing statements and renewal dates because automatic payments are easy to forget.

If a merchant charges after valid cancellation, preserve proof and contact the merchant and payment provider promptly. Do not mislabel an authorised charge as fraud simply because cancellation instructions were misunderstood.

Count a subscription saving only from the first avoided charge. Keep a small “restart” note for services cancelled experimentally; if the household genuinely misses one, restore it deliberately and update the ledger rather than treating the audit as failure.

sections.heading: Compare Insurance Without Hollowing Out the Cover
paragraphs: Insurance can produce a large premium difference, but reducing protection is not the same as finding waste. Compare the same insured people, property, use, limits, excess, add-ons and payment basis before calling one quote cheaper.

Start ahead of renewal rather than allowing automatic renewal to decide. Obtain several quotes through reputable routes and check that every application answer is accurate. An incorrect occupation, mileage, address or claims history can undermine cover.

Annual payment may cost less than monthly instalments, which can involve credit. Compare total payable, not twelve times the boldest monthly figure. Preserve cash for essentials; do not force annual payment if it would require expensive borrowing.

Check duplication through packaged bank accounts, employment benefits, vehicle manufacturers, home policies and credit cards. Breakdown, gadget, travel and legal cover are common overlaps, but policy definitions and eligible people can differ.

Raise an excess only if the household could pay it after a loss. A £120 premium saving paired with an additional £750 excess transfers risk rather than eliminating cost. Record the amount the emergency fund would need.

Remove add-ons only after understanding them. Courtesy car, home emergency, legal expenses and protected no-claims features can be valuable in a specific household. Ask for the premium with and without each item.

Use regulated firms and verify permissions where appropriate. A suspiciously low quote, pressure to provide false details or request to pay a broker through an individual account is a warning, not a bargain.

If circumstances changed—working from home, business use, renovations, an additional driver or valuable equipment—tell the insurer. The audit is an opportunity to correct cover, even when doing so increases the premium.
Calculate net first-year saving after cancellation fees and lost multi-policy discounts. Then note the renewal month and shop again. A competitive introductory premium can become expensive later.
Count the saving only when equivalent or intentionally revised cover is active and the old policy is cancelled on the correct date. Never create an uninsured gap to meet the £200 target.

sections.heading: Check Energy, Water and Council Tax Support Before Cutting Usage
paragraphs: Essential bills need a different audit. First verify the bill is accurate, the tariff or scheme is appropriate and all eligible support is claimed. Only then consider safe consumption changes. Heat, hygiene, food storage and medical needs are not discretionary luxuries.

For energy, record supplier, tariff, unit rates, standing charges, payment method, annual consumption, contract end date and exit fee. Compare using consumption rather than a monthly Direct Debit, because the payment can include credit or recovery of an earlier shortfall.

[[S5|Ofgem publishes]] regional unit rates and standing charges under the price cap and explains that the headline annual figure assumes typical consumption. A cap on rates is not a cap on a household’s total bill.

Submit accurate meter readings where appropriate and reconcile estimated bills. Check whether the account has accumulated an unusually large credit or debt and ask the supplier to explain the Direct Debit calculation before changing it.

If struggling, contact the supplier early. Ask about affordable plans, hardship support and the Priority Services Register where relevant. Cancelling an energy Direct Debit without arranging payment can worsen the problem.

Water support differs by nation and company. Check meter suitability, social tariffs, hardship schemes and billed household details. A meter can help some households and cost others more; use the provider assessment rather than assuming.

Council Tax reductions and exemptions depend on local rules and household circumstances. Check single-person discount, disability-related provisions, student status and Council Tax Reduction through the relevant council. Report changes promptly and do not rely on a generic social-media checklist.

Benefits calculators can identify possible entitlement, but the authority’s decision controls. Keep evidence, application dates and review deadlines. Income support can release more monthly room than cutting many small purchases.

Use efficiency actions that protect health: control unused rooms where safe, reduce draughts, use appropriate appliance settings and avoid wasting hot water. Do not recommend a fixed thermostat setting for every age, property or medical condition.
An essential-bill saving is verified when the new tariff, discount, corrected bill or support award appears. Until then, enter it in the ledger as pending rather than spending the expected amount.

sections.heading: Audit Broadband, Mobile and Pay-TV as One System
paragraphs: Connectivity bills often combine high saving potential with contract risk. List broadband, mobile lines, handset finance, landline, pay-TV, streaming add-ons and equipment rental together. A cheap bundle can still include services the household does not use.

Check whether each service is in or out of its minimum term. Leaving early can trigger an exit charge. End-of-contract notices, account pages and provider support should show the relevant date and available options.

[[S4|Ofcom’s consumer guidance]] recommends checking contract status, shopping around when out of contract, reviewing bundles and matching mobile data to actual use. Eligible customers should also check social tariffs rather than assuming advertised retail offers are the only choice.

Compare coverage and reliability before price. A cheaper mobile network that fails at home or work is not an equivalent service. Use postcode tools, provider information and lived experience from the places where connection matters.

For broadband, compare speed actually needed, not the largest advertised number. Video calls, streaming, gaming, uploads, household size and router placement matter. Keep evidence of current performance before accepting a lower tier.

Separate handset cost from airtime. When handset finance ends, confirm whether the bill falls automatically and whether a SIM-only plan is appropriate. Check remaining device balance before switching.

Ofcom’s 2026 pricing analysis reported that many out-of-contract broadband customers paid roughly £7 to £9 more each month than in-contract customers. That is a market average, not a promised individual saving, but it makes contract status a high-priority check.

Ask the current provider for its best comparable offer, then compare the total minimum-term cost with alternatives. Include setup, delivery, activation, equipment return, annual price changes and any credit that arrives later.

The midpoint photograph shows a router because this category requires a product decision, not merely cancelling entertainment. Connectivity supports work, study, health and access to services, so preserve performance and resilience while removing unused extras.

Document switch date, final bill and equipment return tracking. A quoted £18 monthly reduction is not complete until the old service ends, the new service works and no unreturned-router charge appears.

sections.heading: Recover Fees, Interest and Forgotten Cash
paragraphs: Bank fees and interest can be recurring leaks disguised as consequences. Review overdraft interest, account charges, foreign transaction fees, cash-withdrawal costs, late fees and paid account benefits. The aim is to change the cause, not merely complain about a valid charge.

Move bill dates closer to reliable income where providers allow it. Maintain a small current-account buffer and low-balance alert. Timing changes improve resilience even when they do not count as savings.

A packaged account deserves a benefit audit. List the insurance and services actually eligible and used, compare standalone alternatives, and check whether cancellation affects an arranged overdraft or other feature.

Credit-card interest is not solved by cancelling the Direct Debit. Keep at least the required payment in place and obtain free debt guidance if minimums are unaffordable. Priority household bills may need attention before unsecured overpayments.

Check dormant balances: old savings accounts, app wallets, gift cards, work expenses, refunds, rail delay claims and utility credits. These are one-off recoveries, not monthly savings, so track them separately.

Review tax code and payslip for obvious changes, but use HMRC’s official services or qualified help rather than estimating a refund from an advert. Never pay an unverified claims company a large percentage for a task available directly.

Challenge unauthorised or duplicate transactions promptly through the appropriate merchant and payment-provider process. Preserve dates, amounts and evidence. Do not count a disputed sum as recovered until credited finally.

When a lender or provider offers a short promotional period, record the end date and standard price. A balance transfer, fee waiver or free account can become expensive if the follow-up action is missed.

Direct recovered cash toward the reason for the audit: bill buffer, priority arrears, expensive debt or a defined goal. Treating a £300 refund as £25 monthly saving would overstate the sustainable result.
This category is complete when recurring fees are prevented, one-off money is labelled separately and essential payment protections remain intact.

sections.heading: Use the Cancellation Ladder to Protect Essentials
paragraphs: Rank candidates by harm if removed. Level one is forgotten, duplicated or clearly unused. Level two is convenient but replaceable. Level three supports work, care, health or household functioning. Level four is legally or contractually essential. Start at level one.
For every cancellation, answer four questions: Is there a contract balance? Does anyone else rely on it? Must data or records be exported? Is replacement cover or service required before closure?

Pause before cutting home internet, mobile access, transport, childcare, professional fees or software used to earn income. A saving that reduces earning capacity can be deeply negative even if the statement becomes smaller.

Priority obligations require early contact rather than silent non-payment. MoneyHelper’s bill prioritiser can help distinguish consequences, and free debt advisers can assist when there is no affordable configuration.

Avoid “cancel the card” tactics. Recurring payments may migrate to a replacement card, and an unpaid contract can remain enforceable. Use the merchant’s documented route and the payment-provider rights that apply.
Preserve evidence: confirmation number, transcript, email, screenshot, postal proof and equipment tracking. Put the final charge and expected refund in the calendar. Check the next two statements.

If cancellation creates a service gap, schedule replacement first. Insurance should overlap correctly; broadband switching should follow the regulated process; prescriptions and care services require continuity.
Households should agree on shared cuts. Give each person a small protected preference where possible. A budget imposed on one person while another retains every convenience is unlikely to last.
Use a reversible trial for borderline services: downgrade, pause or remove auto-renewal while retaining access to the end date. If the household does not miss the service, complete cancellation.
The ladder protects against false economy. It turns a frantic target into a sequence in which the easiest, safest pounds are claimed before quality of life or security is weakened.

sections.heading: Negotiate With a Script, Then Read the Offer
paragraphs: Provider calls work better with a prepared request. State the current product, contract position and comparable offer, then ask for the lowest total cost that preserves the required service. Silence and precision are more useful than threatening to leave immediately.

Ask the agent to identify the new minimum term, monthly price, setup or administration fees, included features, future price changes and cooling-off rights. A verbal “saving” is incomplete until these elements are clear.
Do not invent a competitor quote. Use a dated, genuinely available offer and note whether it is limited to new customers, a postcode, payment method or bundle. The provider may match only part of it.

If the first offer is weak, ask whether there is a better tariff or a specialist retention team. Remain polite and end the call if pressure replaces explanation. A decision can wait until written terms arrive.

Request accessible communication or an authorised representative process when needed. Providers may have support for vulnerability, language, disability or financial difficulty; asking is not a negotiation failure.

After the call, compare total term cost rather than the first-month discount. Save the order summary and cancellation deadline. If the written terms differ from the call, raise the discrepancy before the cooling-off window closes.
For a household service, confirm with other users before accepting slower speed, fewer channels or a lower allowance. A retention deal that creates an immediate upgrade later may cost more overall.
Record “no change” when the current deal remains best. An audit is successful when it avoids a bad switch as well as when it reduces a bill. Do not force every call to produce a saving.

sections.heading: Turn Candidates Into a £200 Decision Ledger
paragraphs: Create columns for current monthly cost, new monthly cost, one-off cost, start date, confidence and status. Use “identified,” “requested,” “confirmed” and “visible on statement.” Only the last two belong in a spending plan.

An illustrative ledger might show £35 from cancelled subscriptions, £18 from broadband, £22 from mobile lines, £28 from equivalent insurance, £17 from bank fees, £45 from groceries and £35 from other bills. The £200 total is an example, not evidence that every household can reproduce it.
Calculate first-year net value: twelve months of recurring reduction minus exit, setup, postage and equipment costs. For a change beginning in three months, do not pretend the saving exists today.

Separate one-off recoveries in another box. Refunds, account credit and sold belongings can fund a buffer but do not support a new recurring commitment. Never use them to justify a higher monthly bill.

Add confidence labels. High means confirmed in writing; medium means quoted but not implemented; low means an estimate or potential eligibility. Build the revised budget from high-confidence items only.

Assign each verified pound before it disappears. Options include priority arrears, a £100–£500 starter buffer, expensive debt, an annual-bill sinking fund or a defined goal. The best destination depends on consequences and household stability.

Do not celebrate £200 of cuts by taking on a £200 finance agreement. Wait for two statement cycles, then decide how much is genuinely recurring. Some savings will be offset by annual increases or a replacement service.
Schedule renewal alerts and quarterly statement scans. The audit is maintenance, not a one-time purge. New trials and price rises enter quietly, while old assumptions stop matching use.

If the confirmed total is below £200, preserve it. The remaining gap may require income, benefit entitlement, debt restructuring or housing and transport decisions that cannot be solved in ten minutes.
The ledger succeeds when every number is traceable to a bill, contract or confirmation and when the household knows where the released cash will go.

sections.heading: Verify the Result Across Two Statements
paragraphs: On day one, complete the ten-minute scan and choose the three largest safe candidates. During week one, collect terms, compare like with like and submit changes. Keep complex essential bills separate from instant cancellations.

At the next statement, confirm cancelled payments stopped, final bills are correct, replacement services work and promised credits arrived. Investigate unexpected debits immediately but remember that a valid final contractual charge may still be due.

At the second statement, total only recurring differences. Compare equivalent periods and account for seasonal energy, irregular groceries and annual bills. A quieter month is not necessarily a structural saving.

Check service quality. Slower broadband, failed mobile coverage, inadequate insurance or repeated grocery top-ups indicate that the cheaper configuration is not equivalent. Correct it before the inconvenience becomes a crisis.

Review the destination account. If savings were intended for a buffer or debt but remained in everyday spending, automate a transfer just after income arrives. Use an amount below the verified total to leave margin for variation.
Keep a cancellation archive for at least as long as disputes or final bills remain possible. Redact and dispose of obsolete documents securely under the household’s retention needs.

Repeat a five-minute scan monthly and a deeper review before major renewals. Do not spend hours switching a £2 service while ignoring a £40 out-of-contract bill; keep ranking by annual value and risk.
Use a second adult or trusted adviser for high-stakes changes. A fresh reader may spot duplicated cover, an exclusion or an exit fee that excitement missed.
If bills remain unaffordable after safe reductions, seek free, independent support early. The honest conclusion may be that costs cannot be cut enough without help or an income change.
The method is complete when the statement—not a quotation—shows the reduction, essential services remain sound and the released cash has a durable job.

sections.heading: Price Groceries by Meals, Waste and Unit Cost
paragraphs: Food spending is visible and emotionally charged, but it should not carry the entire savings target. Start with waste, convenience premiums and unplanned top-up trips before reducing nutrition or culturally important foods.
Use receipts from several normal weeks. Group staple meals, fresh food, snacks, drinks, takeaways, delivery fees and household goods. A single celebration or stock-up week is not a useful baseline.

Plan a short list of meals around food already at home, then make a list by aisle. Check cupboards and freezer before shopping. The late photograph shows a shopper using a phone beside a produce-filled trolley because the useful tool is a live list and price check at the decision point.
Compare unit prices, not package price alone. A larger pack is cheaper only if it is consumed before spoilage and does not push the basket over available cash. Promotions can increase total spend.

Choose swaps selectively. Store brands can reduce cost in staples; some premium or specialist products may be worth keeping. Test one substitution at a time so the household learns what it will actually use.

Calculate takeaway and meal-delivery cost including fees, tips and unused groceries displaced by the order. A planned convenience meal may prevent a more expensive order, so build realistic low-effort options into the week.
Use loyalty prices only after comparing the underlying price and data trade-off. A points balance is not cash, and buying extra to reach a reward is not saving.

Protect nutritional and medical requirements. Food allergies, diabetes, pregnancy, disability, eating-disorder history and limited cooking facilities change what “cheap” means. Seek appropriate professional or local support when food is unaffordable.
Set a weekly spending guide with room for price variation. If a lower target causes repeated midweek top-ups, use the true total. Sustainable meal routines matter more than an impressive first shop.
Count grocery savings against a four-week or monthly baseline only after several comparable weeks. Waste avoided and delivery fees removed are often more durable than extreme restriction.

summary: Treat £200 as a search target, not a guaranteed result. Run a ten-minute discovery scan across current-account and credit-card statements, regular-payment lists and renewal emails. Record merchants, monthly equivalents and next dates without cancelling immediately.

Sort each item into keep, cancel after checking, renegotiate or switch, investigate, and protect. Begin with forgotten, duplicated and clearly unused services. Protect housing, Council Tax, energy, essential connectivity, work costs, required insurance and priority debts.

Convert all costs to the same monthly basis. Divide annual bills by twelve and multiply weekly costs by 52 before dividing by twelve. Separate genuine annual savings from cash-flow changes, introductory discounts, cashback and one-off refunds.

Build evidence for large candidates: bill, contract end date, notice period, usage, payment method, exit fee and comparable replacement. Stopping a Direct Debit or recurring card payment does not necessarily end the underlying contract.

Review subscriptions and annual renewals, but preserve shared data and ask household members before cancelling. Record the final service date and confirmation. A deletion of an app or card does not reliably cancel a subscription.

Audit broadband, mobile, handset finance, pay-TV and streaming together. Compare coverage, required speed, equipment costs, annual price changes and total minimum-term price. Check contract status and social-tariff eligibility.

Compare insurance on equivalent cover, excess, insured people and use. Annual payment may be cheaper, but only if cash is available without expensive borrowing. Never create a gap in required or important cover.

For energy, water and Council Tax, verify bills, tariff, household details, meter information and support eligibility before reducing safe consumption. The energy price cap limits rates for covered tariffs, not a household’s total bill.

Review overdraft interest, account fees, late charges and paid account benefits. Keep required debt payments in place and seek free guidance if bills or minimums are unaffordable. Track refunds and dormant balances as one-off recoveries, not monthly savings.

Use a cancellation ladder: unused items first, conveniences second, services supporting work or care third, and legal or contractual essentials last. Confirm who relies on each service, what data must be exported and whether replacement is needed.

For groceries, compare several normal weeks. Reduce waste, delivery fees and unplanned top-ups before cutting nutrition. Plan meals around food already held, use a live shopping list and compare unit prices rather than package headlines.

Maintain a decision ledger with current cost, replacement cost, one-off fee, start date, confidence and status. Count only confirmed changes, and build the revised budget from savings visible on statements.
Check two statement cycles and service quality before treating the total as permanent. Direct verified room toward priority arrears, a starter buffer, costly debt, annual bills or a defined goal.

If the result is below £200, keep the verified amount. The remaining gap may require benefit checks, free debt support, income action or larger housing and transport decisions rather than unsafe cuts.

Prepare provider calls with the current deal, contract end date, usage and a real comparable quote. Ask for total minimum-term cost, fees, annual increases and cooling-off terms. Do not accept a first-month discount as proof of a cheaper contract.

Record the result of every call, including a decision to keep the current service. Avoiding a weaker switch is a valid audit result. Save order summaries and compare written terms with what the agent said before any cancellation window closes.

Make shared decisions visibly. Confirm who uses subscriptions, connectivity, insurance and storage before changing them, and export files where needed. A household saving that surprises another user or destroys access is not safely implemented.

Keep one-off recoveries separate from recurring savings. A refund, sold item or returned account credit can strengthen the buffer, but it cannot support a new monthly commitment or make the ongoing ledger look larger.

faq.question: Can every household find £200 a month?
faq.answer: No. £200 is a search target; only verified reductions that fit the household should be counted.

faq.question: Does cancelling a Direct Debit cancel the contract?
faq.answer: Usually not. It stops the payment instruction, while contractual charges may remain due.

faq.question: Which costs should be checked first?
faq.answer: Start with unused subscriptions, duplicated cover and high-value contracts that are outside their minimum term.

faq.question: How should an annual bill be compared?
faq.answer: Divide total annual cost by twelve and include instalment interest, fees, excess and coverage differences.

faq.question: When does a quoted saving become real?
faq.answer: When the change is confirmed and appears correctly on a bill or statement without unacceptable loss of service.

faq.question: What if essential bills are unaffordable?
faq.answer: Prioritise consequences and contact the provider or a free independent debt adviser early rather than cancelling payment silently.

glossary.definition: A common monthly figure used to compare weekly, four-weekly and annual costs.
Authority for an organisation to collect variable or fixed amounts from a bank account.
A scheduled bank payment controlled by the account holder.
Permission for a merchant to charge a payment card repeatedly.
The contractual period during which early exit charges may apply.
Cost per standard quantity such as kilogram, litre or item.
An obligation whose non-payment can have especially serious consequences.
Recurring reductions in year one after setup, exit and other one-off costs.
